📊 How Big Are Dolphin Pods? (259 Counted Pods, 2021–2026)
Most dolphins travel in small pairs, trios, or nursery groups (2–6 dolphins), though big social pods occasionally gather at tidal passes:








🧬 Fast Facts: Sarasota Bay’s Resident Dolphins
Long-term dorsal-fin tracking of 482 resident Sarasota Bay dolphins (Wells et al., 2025) reveals:

Homebodies for life: ~160–170 core residents live in Sarasota Bay in any given year, and almost nobody moves in or out (< 1.3% immigration per year).
Long lives: Females live up to 67 years and males up to 52 years.
Calving season: 81% of babies are born in May–July, and calves stay closely bonded with their moms for 3 to 6 years.

🐟 Fish Funnels + Easy Views

Dolphin buffet: Strong tides rush through Big Sarasota Pass, New Pass, and Venice Inlet, funneling mullet and pinfish right into dolphin hunting lanes.
Human vantage points: Bridges, piers, and jetty walkways sit right beside those passes—making it super easy for people on shore to snap photos!

title: 🌦️ Why Sightings Drop in Late Summer
text:
🐬 The Big Surprise: Sightings peak in March and drop by over two-thirds in August–October—yet Sarasota Bay’s dolphins stay in the bay all 12 months of the year! What actually changes is human weather: late-summer heat, afternoon lightning storms, and hurricane season keep people off the water.








🔑 Two Reasons Behind the Curve

Spring Tourism + Calm Seas (Jan–Apr): Cool, sunny dry-season weather puts thousands of boaters and beachgoers along Sarasota Bay’s passes.
Summer Moms & Calves (May–Jul) vs. Storm Season (Aug–Oct): Even though 81% of calves are born in May–July (Wells et al., 2025), late-summer storms push people indoors while underwater hydrophones still hear dolphins whistling away!

title: 📈 2021–2026 Trends & Major Hurricanes
text:
🌀 Storms vs. Survival: Notice how sightings dip right when major hurricanes hit (Ian in 2022, Idalia in 2023, Helene & Milton in 2024)—then bounce right back the next spring! Resident Sarasota Bay dolphins stay put through hurricanes while damaged piers and marinas temporarily slow human sightings.








📌 Why Did Overall Sightings Climb From 2021 to 2026?

More smartphone cameras, stable dolphin numbers: Suncoast sightings nearly doubled from 98 in 2021 to 179 in 2026 mainly because more people log wildlife on apps like iNaturalist.
Balanced population: Wells et al. (2025) found Sarasota Bay’s annual birth rate (7.1%) almost perfectly matches its annual loss rate (7.2%), keeping the community remarkably steady!

title: 🐬 About This Project
text:
📂 Data Source
All maps and charts on this site analyze 2,206 research-grade, GPS-verified visual sightings of common bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) recorded across Florida from January 2021 through October 2026—including 207 sightings inside the Sarasota Bay study area—downloaded from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) via iNaturalist community observations. Biological context on Sarasota Bay’s year-round resident population, May–July calving season, and 67-year lifespans comes from peer-reviewed dorsal-fin tracking by Wells et al. (2025) and the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program.

title: 🌦️☀️ Seasons & Time of Day (2021–2026)
text:
🐬 One Big Weather Story: Sarasota Bay’s dolphins live in the bay 24 hours a day, all 12 months of the year—yet sightings swing dramatically by both season and clock hour because human boaters and beachgoers follow cool sunshine and avoid darkness, summer heat, and lightning storms!


🌦️ 1. Across the Seasons: Why Sightings Drop in Late Summer
Sightings peak in March during Florida’s sunny dry season and drop by over two-thirds in August–October during storm and hurricane season—even though 81% of Sarasota Bay calves are born in May–July (Wells et al., 2025):









⏰ 2. Across the Clock: Sightings Hour-by-Hour
Sightings surge between 10:00 AM and 4:00 PM when people are out on boats and piers, while underwater microphones prove dolphins keep hunting and whistling right through the night (click any coastal zone in the legend to filter!):









🌤️ 3. Where Seasons & Time of Day Meet: Morning vs. Afternoon
Notice how the two patterns connect: in Summer, boaters head out early (Morning: 45.7%) to beat afternoon heat and lightning storms, whereas in Winter, mild sunny Afternoons (51.9%) take the lead!

⚠️ Three Quick Rules for Reading Dolphin Data

More photos ≠ more dolphins: Citizen sightings go up when beaches, piers, and boats are busy (sunny spring afternoons) and drop during summer storms or hurricanes—even though Sarasota Bay’s resident dolphins stay home all year!
Sightings vs. unique dolphins: The same friendly Sarasota Bay dolphin can be photographed dozens of times across 2021–2026, so 2,206 sightings means 2,206 encounters, not 2,206 different animals.
Honest missing values: When an observer didn’t count the exact pod size (1,947 sightings) or didn’t log a clock hour (105 sightings), we leave it blank rather than guessing.

title: 🐬 Florida & Sarasota Bay Bottlenose Dolphins
text:
🔍 What This Graph Shows—and Why Sightings Rise and Fall
This interactive chart combines 2,206 verified wild bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) sightings recorded along Florida’s coastlines from January 2021 through October 2026 (hover over any color bar or click a coastal zone in the legend to isolate it!). At first glance, you might think Florida’s dolphins migrate away every late summer—sightings soar to 343 in April during sunny dry-season weather, stay lively into May–July peak calving season (when over 81% of Sarasota Bay dolphin calves are born), and then plunge by more than half in August–October.
Here is the scientific twist: long-term dorsal-fin tracking shows that Sarasota Bay’s ~160–170 resident dolphins stay in their home bay all 12 months of the year! What actually changes across the calendar is human observer effort. Cool, calm winter and spring afternoons bring thousands of boaters, kayakers, and pier visitors out with cameras, whereas scorching late-summer heat, daily afternoon lightning storms, and major Gulf hurricanes push people indoors while dolphins keep hunting and whistling below the waves.
